hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? in a conversation, are you more of a talker or a listener?
options: me too, some days. you’re about to meet a young man like that.
then zeno would have liked you.
fair. watch what zeno says about it.

steps.line: Zeno didn’t teach in a private school. He taught in a public place, where people passed all day: the edge of the marketplace in Athens.
He taught under a stoa, a long porch of columns. His was the painted porch, its walls covered in famous paintings of battles.

steps.q: Zeno came to philosophy by accident. What brought him to Athens, the old story says?
o: A shipwreck, with a cargo of dye
A prize for winning a race
steps.why: Diogenes Laertius says the merchant from Cyprus was shipwrecked, read about Socrates in an Athens bookshop, and asked where men like that were. Crates was walking by.

steps.line: At first his followers were called Zenonians. But the name that stuck was the place: people of the stoa. The Stoics.
Anyone could stop and listen, and anyone could talk. One day a young man wouldn’t stop talking, mostly nonsense.

steps.q: How does Zeno answer the chatterbox?
o: He makes a joke about ears
He asks him to teach instead
steps.why: A joke, with a lesson inside. Diogenes Laertius, who collected the old philosophers’ sayings, kept this one.

steps.line: Zeno said: “The reason we have two ears and only one mouth is that we may listen more and talk less.”

steps.q: Zeno was shy when young. His teacher, Crates, cured it in a strange way. How?
o: Made him give a speech in the market
Made him sing in the theater
Made him carry soup through town
steps.why: Crates handed him a pot of lentil soup to carry, then smashed it with his staff. “Why run away, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you.”

steps.q: Why does it fit that the Stoics were named after an open porch, not a private garden?
o: Their teaching was for life in public
Their teaching was secret, for members
Zeno had no house of his own
steps.why: The market, the courts, the family: that was their classroom. Wisdom in the open.

steps.line: Athens honored him for a life that matched his words. They even trusted him with the keys to the city walls.
Today: lunch in a busy plaza, a friend mid-story. Two ears, one mouth. Let them finish. Wisdom in the open.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Centuries later, which Roman emperor kept a Stoic notebook to himself?
steps.why: Marcus Aurelius wrote his Meditations as notes to himself. Nero had a Stoic tutor too, Seneca, which shows a porch can’t do all the work.

say: here’s what i love. other schools met in groves outside the city, or in a private garden. zeno taught in a public porch on the marketplace, where anyone might pass.

the stoics taught living well right in the middle of life: the market, the courts, the family. zeno said well-being comes little by little, and yet it’s no little thing. every time someone says stoic, they’re pointing at that porch.

steps.q: Today “stoic” often means a stiff face that feels nothing. From this lesson, what did it first mean?
o: Someone who lives apart from the crowd
Someone living wisely, out in public
steps.why: People of the porch. Not cold, but steady, out in the open with everyone else.

today.say: today, in one ordinary conversation, at lunch, at work, on the phone, try zeno’s two ears: listen twice as much as you talk. let the other person finish, then wait one breath before you answer.
options: it’s hard for most people. one conversation is enough.

sources: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.5: Zeno taught walking up and down in the Painted Colonnade (Stoa Poikile); his followers were first called Zenonians, then Stoics, from the place.
Diogenes Laërtius 7.6 (the Athenians deposited the keys of the city walls with him); 7.10–12 (the decree honoring him, his life a pattern in harmony with his teaching).

Diogenes Laërtius 7.23 (to a youth talking nonsense: “The reason why we have two ears and only one mouth is that we may listen the more and talk the less,” R. D. Hicks, 1925); 7.26 (well-being is attained little by little, and yet it is no little thing).
Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.15 (the paintings of the Stoa Poikile, including the Battle of Marathon).

Diogenes Laërtius 7.5 says Zeno chose the Stoa partly to keep it clear of idlers, and 7.14 that he avoided crowds; the lesson now says only that it was a public place where anyone might pass (the earlier “no money” and “busiest spot” were dropped, since 7.13 reports he had means). Confirm.
Teach: “other schools met in groves outside the city, or in a private garden” (the Academy, the Lyceum, Epicurus’s Garden). Confirm.
“Athens honored him for a life that matched his words” paraphrases the decree in 7.10–11; the keys are from 7.6. Confirm the order and wording.
Teach: “well-being comes little by little, and yet it’s no little thing” (7.26) is attributed to Zeno. Confirm.
